name: Babole
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Leitch, Myles. 2003. Babole (C101). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu languages, 392-421. London/New York: Routledge. [corroborated by Leitch, Myles. 2014. Stem tone dynamics of Dibole, a Bantu C language. Africana Linguistica 20: 207-224, DOI 10.3406/aflin.2014.1031, open access on Persée]
catalog_locator: §2.3 'Tone in nominal forms' and §2.4 'Tone and prosodic structure of verb roots/stems', p. 398. Corroboration: Leitch 2014 §2 'Overview of Tonal Dynamics', pp. 208-209 (scan).
catalog_quote: Babole displays the classic Bantu pattern of four basic tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems; HL, HH, LL, LH. These four patterns are more or less equally represented in the nominal lexicon with no pattern being dominant and no gaps occurring. Nominal prefixes are always low-toned and so I do not represent tone on noun prefixes in this chapter. ... The structure of Babole verbs is such that a lexical tone (High or Low) is always associated with the initial verb root syllable. The tone-bearing unit (TBU) is the syllable in Babole and there is no contrastive vowel length. Depending on the tense/mode/aspect involved, the subsequent syllables of the stem will have particular tonal properties as sketched in the section on verbal stem morphology.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (1,561 lines; pypdf text of the Routledge chapter, printed pp. 392-421). Both halves of the reported quote are there word for word: §2.3 'Tone in nominal forms', p. 398 (the text): "Babole displays the classic Bantu pattern of four basic tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems; HL, HH, LL, LH. These four patterns are more or less equally represented in the nominal lexicon with no pattern being dominant and no gaps occurring. Nominal prefixes are always low-toned and so I do not represent tone on noun prefixes in this chapter." and §2.4 'Tone and prosodic structure of verb roots/stems', p. 398 (lines 359-361): "The structure of Babole verbs is such that…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dibole/Babole is a two-tone (H/L) register-tone language: noun stems carry lexically contrastive tone patterns (four melodies on disyllabic stems), verb roots carry a lexical H or L on the root-initial syllable with the remaining stem syllables receiving tone from TMA suffixal melodies; the TBU is the syllable and vowel length is not contrastive. The chapter never mentions stress, accent, or any culminative prominence; no stress rule is stated and none can be inferred.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none discussed). Tonal complications: downstep after negation -ká-, tonal melodies under relativization, deverbal-noun suffix tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tonal description (noun stems, verb stems); the word 'stress' does not occur in the chapter. Data from the author's fieldwork in the village of Dzeke (Central dialect area). Confidence 'medium' only because the source is silent on stress rather than explicitly denying it.
new_statements.identity_note: Leitch's 'Babole' = Glottolog dibo1245 Dibole (ISO bvx; alt. names Babole, Southern Bomitaba), Bantu C101 (Guthrie C10; Motingea in the same volume calls it 'Babole-Dzeke C14'). Leitch's data come from three years' residence in the village of Dzeke (Central of the three dialect areas North/Central/South he distinguishes). No separate glottocode for the Dzeke variety.

new_statements.quote: Vowel length is not contrastive in Dibole. Morpheme internal vowel hiatus is commonplace and even V,-V,, sequences with identical vowel qualities in V, and V, are uniformly interpreted as distinct Tone Bearning Units (TBUs). [...] In general, there are no contour tones on singleton vowels. [p. 208] All verb roots, like those in (1), are lexically specified with either a High (H) or Low (L) tone. This tone is realized uniquely on the initial verb root vowel. The non-initial syllables in the root, and any TBUs added by extending the root with various suffixes, are represented as underlyingly toneless except for the Final Vowel (FV). [p. 209] In the Imperative smgulars where there is no prefix, the surface forms are audibly lengthened. These two phenomena taken together suggest a minimally binary word condition for Dibole. [p. 213]
new_statements.citation: Leitch, Myles. 2014. Stem tone dynamics of Dibole, a Bantu C language. Africana Linguistica 20: 207-224.
new_statements.locator: §2 'Overview of Tonal Dynamics', pp. 208-209; minimal-word remark §4 p. 213

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Leitch 2003 statement (tone language, no stress statement): fully tonal description, no stress remark. Adds tonal detail only (each vowel a TBU, no length contrast, root-initial lexical tone, minimal binary word), none of it about stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone article only. Dibole is described as a tone language with every vowel a TBU, no contrastive vowel length, no contour tones on single vowels, a lexical H or L on the root-initial vowel and toneless non-initial stem syllables that take a melodic tone from the final vowel; a minimally binary (two-syllable) word condition is inferred from lengthening of prefixless CV imperatives. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the article (only 'accent aigu/grave' in the abbreviations list, p. 224); nothing is said about word stress or non-tonal prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: none (the paper is about verb-stem tone melodies and metatony)
new_statements.identity_note: Leitch 2014 describes the variety of the villages Dzeke and Impongui, 'the northernmost of 3 dialect areas' (p. 208); Leitch 2003 (catalog source) covers the same Impongui/Dzeke variety of the Northern dialect area (p. 393). The 1996/97 thesis uses the author's own Babole field data (C-10) without naming a dialect; its stress remarks are about Bantu C generally and about Bobangi, Londengese, Ntomba and Bolia specifically.

sources.citation: Leitch, Myles Francis. 1996 [dated 1997 by the author]. Vowel Harmonies of the Congo Basin: An Optimality Theory Analysis of Variation in the Bantu Zone C. PhD thesis, University of British Columbia. 282 pp.
sources.note: 282-page monograph with the fullest Babole phonology (segments, syllable, harmony) by the only descriptive linguist of the language; the most likely place for an explicit remark on stress or its absence. UBC retrospective theses are normally open on cIRcle, but the site's bot defence served a captcha to every request here.
